title: Moraxella, Kingella, and Other Gram-Negative Cocci

questions.stem: A 66-year-old man presented with a 1-week history of cough, pleuritic chest pain, and low-grade fevers. He was known to have chronic obstructive pulmonary disorder and had a smoking pack year history of 60 years. Investigations: CXR revealed a dense infiltrate in the right lower lobe Sputum microscopy revealed numerous gram-negative cocci, many in pairs
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate therapy?
questions.explanation: Amoxicillin/clavulanate In addition to Haemophilus influenzae and Streptococcus pneumoniae, Moraxella catarrhalis is a common cause of exacerbations of COPD. The Gram stain depicts gramnegative cocci in pairs, typical of Moraxella catarrhalis. The best answer choice would be amoxicillin/clavulanate due to increasing resistance noted to TMP–SMX and tetracyclines for Moraxella. Amoxicillin/clavulanate would be preferred over a quinolone.

questions.question: Multiple anal ulcers.

parts.text: Name 2 possible organisms causing this.

questions.model_answer: Two possible organisms causing multiple anal ulcers: herpes simplex virus (HSV-2 most commonly, proctitis in receptive anal intercourse) and Treponema pallidum (primary syphilis chancre, can be multiple in anal location); also consider lymphogranuloma venereum (Chlamydia trachomatis L1-L3 serovars).

questions.question: 13. 40-year old HIV + patient has a positive EIA for T. pallidum. He was never screened prior to now, and never received treatment for syphilis. He had an anaphylactic reaction to cefixime 2 years ago when treated for gonorrhea.

parts.text: List 3 possible indications for a lumbar puncture in this patient
c) List 3 tests you would ask for on cerebrospinal fluid.
d) He is diagnosed with neurosyphilis. Name 2 important elements of your antimicrobial therapeutic approach for this patient (be precise – dose, duration, etc.)
e) List 2 laboratory criteria that would indicate a failure of your treatment

cohort_answer.text: Canadian STI guidelines indications for LP: Presence of neurologic or ophthalmic symptoms/signs; Congenital syphilis; Previously treated patients who fail to achieve adequate serologic response; Tertiary syphilis; HIV patients with neurologic symptoms/signs; Late latent syphilis; RPR≥1:32 dilutions, CD4<350 or treated syphilis with suboptimal decline in VDRL/RPR titre. Some experts recommend CSF exam in all HIV-infected individuals and all patients with RPR≥1:32. CSF tests: VDRL (most specific); Cell count with differential; Protein. Treatment: skin test for penicillin -> if negative treat with penicillin, if positive consider desensitization then treat with penicillin (less data on CTX efficacy for neurosyphilis). Regimens: Aqueous crystalline penicillin G IV 3-4 million units q4hr x10-14d; Ceftriaxone 2g IV/IM q24hr x10-14d. Failure criteria: CSF VDRL rising 2 dilutions or more; CSF WBC fails to resolve (usually first to improve). Other criteria: clinical progression; at 2yr post-treatment still persistently abnormal CSF WBC or VDRL positive; persistently low CSF VDRL titre.

questions.question: You see a patient who has been treated adequately for syphilis two years ago. He has a negative RPR and a positive treponemal test. He still has risk factors.

parts.text: Named 4 reason why the treponemal test may be persistent

cohort_answer.text: Treated syphilis; Early primary syphilis; Tertiary syphilis; Late latent syphilis; Endemic treponemal infection (not in this patient)
